pañcāṅga
(‘[the almanac which has] five limbs’)
------------------------------------------
Vedic sacrifices were very common even in the most ancient period. However, they had to be performed at certain times considered as auspicious based on the astronomical position of स्तर्स् and प्लनेत्स्. Thus evolved the science of Hindu Almanac, called ‘pañcāṅga’.
Literally, the word means ‘five limbs’. These five limbs of the पञ्चाङ्ग are:
Vāra or day of the week.
Tithi or lunar day.
Nakṣatra or the lunar mansion.
Karaṇa or half a tithi.
Yoga or the time during which the sun and the मोओन् together accomplish 13 degrees and 20 minutes of space.
Vāra is the day of the week (the solar day or the civil day). A day is the period between two sunrises. This period, again, is divided into ahan (= day, from sunrise to sunset) and रात्रि (= night, from sunset to sunrise). The week comprises seven days named after the seven प्लनेत्स्: bhānu or the sun, सोम or the मोओन्, मङ्गल or the mars, बुध or the mercury, गुरु or the जुपितेर्, शुक्र or the venus and शनि or the saturn.
The day and the night are further divided into 15 muhūrtas each, a मुहूर्त having a duration of 48 minutes. Half a मुहूर्त is called ghaṭikā (= 24 minutes).
Tithi is one lunar day. It is defined as the day in which the मोओन्, leaving the sun (at the last moment of अमावास्या or new-मोओन्) traverses twelve degrees towards the east, every day.
The tithis are counted from the day next to amāvāsya as pratipad (first), dvitīyā (second), tṛtīyā (third) and so on, up to the fifteenth which is pūrṇimā or full-मोओन् day. The same calculation is continued after that, in the same way, ending with the अमावास्या or the new-मोओन् day.
The first fortnight is called śuklapakṣa (bright fortnight) and the second, kṛṣṇapakṣa (dark fortnight). Consequently a tithi has to be qualified by this also. For instance, the fourth day after अमावास्या is śukla-caturthī. The eighth day after pūrṇimā is कृष्ण-aṣṭamī.
Though the exact duration of a lunar day is of 60 ghaṭikās (equal to 24 hours), the motion of the मोओन् being irregular, this traversing of twelve degrees varies from 54 to 65 ghaṭikās. Consequently there may be two tithis on the same unit day or the same tithi can extend over two unit days.
Nakṣatra (= star or constellation) is actually the lunar mansion. It is the name of 1∕27 part of the path of the मोओन् round the earth which comes to 13⅓ degrees of the sky. Though the मोओन् travels through a little less than one नक्षत्र everyday, the day can be called as having that नक्षत्र for that day. The नक्षत्र in its turn is named after a prominent star or constellation nearby.
Twenty-seven nakṣatras (from अश्विनी to Revatī) have been recognised by the astronomical works and incorporated into the pañcāṅgas also. (See NAKṢATRA for details.)
The next item is karaṇa. It is half of a tithi. Hence there are 60 karaṇas in a lunar month of 30 tithis.
The karaṇas are only of astrological use and have been given different names which are eleven in number. Out of them seven are cara (= moving) and four are sthira (= stationary).
The cara-karaṇas are: bava, bālava, kaulava, taitila, gara, vaṇija and विष्टि.
The sthira-karaṇas are: शकुनि, catuṣpāda, नाग and kiṁstughna.
In a lunar month there are two pakṣas or fortnights (śukla and कृष्ण). In each पक्ष, on each of the days (like pratipad, dvitīyā and so on) there are two karaṇas. The sthira-karaṇas come only at the end of the kṛṣṇapakṣa whereas the cara-karaṇas rotate in both the pakṣas, the series of seven getting repeated. For instance, after विष्टि (also known as bhadra or kalyāṇī) come bava, bālava and so on.
The following table gives an idea as to how many times these cara-karaṇas occur in a lunar month:
bava 2 9 16 23 30 37 44 51
bālava 3 10 17 24 31 38 45 52
kaulava 4 11 18 25 32 39 46 53
taitila 5 12 19 26 33 40 47 54
gara 6 13 20 27 34 41 48 55
vaṇija 7 14 21 28 35 42 49 56
viṣṭi 8 15 22 29 36 43 50 57

The numbers indicate the serial number in the series (1-60 karaṇas).
The sthira-karaṇas get the numbers as follows: शकुनि (58); catuṣpāda (59); नाग (60); kiṁstughna (1).
Works on अस्त्रोलोग्य् indicate what type of actions can be performed and what should not be done when these karaṇas occur. For instance, bava is auspicious for religious acts that conduce to good health; taitila for building a होउसे.
The seventh karaṇa विष्टि is consi-dered as terrible and forbidden for all auspicious acts.
The last item योग is defined as the time taken by the sun and the मोओन् together to traverse 13° 20’ of space.
When this amounts to 13° 20’, the योग called viṣkambha ends. When it is 26° 40’, the second योग called prīti ends and so on.
There are 27 yogas (making a total of 360°) each of which is given a separate name. These very names describe their nature also. For example: śūla, the 9th योग is like a spear. Śobhana, the 5th is auspicious. Each योग is said to be presided over by a deity. For instance: viṣkambha (1st) by यम; prīti (2nd) by विष्णु; siddhi (16th) by गणेश and so on.
Nine of these yogas like parigha (19th), व्यतीपात (17th) and vidhṛti (27th) are considered very inauspicious and hence condemned.
The system of योग is said to be very ancient.
There are numerous pañcāṅgas in vogue today, being followed by the various sections of the Hindu society. Though scientific-minded astronomers like Varāha-mihira (A.

-587) tried to update their works to accord with the actual positions of the स्तर्स् and the प्लनेत्स् during their times, others do not seem to have done it. As a result, several anomalies have crept into the present-day pañcāṅgas. For instance the मकर सङ्क्रान्ति (the date of the sun leaving the zodiacal sign धनुस् or Sagittarius and entering the sign मकर or Capricorn) is being celebrated on the 14 January every year, though the actual transit takes place on the 21st December itself, thus pushing it forward by 23 days!
The Government of India appointed a committee called the चलेन्दर् Reform Committee in A.
, with Dr. Meghanād Saha (A.

-1956) as its chairman. After examining all the existing calendars, the committee submitted its proposals in November 1955 for an accurate and uniform चलेन्दर् for the whole of India. The proposals covered both the civil चलेन्दर् and the religious चलेन्दर्.
The following are the important recommendations of the committee:
The Śaka era should be used in the unified national चलेन्दर्. The Śaka year 1876 corresponds to 1954-55 A. D.
The year should start from the day following the vernal equinox day.
Normal year is to consist of 365 days, while a leap year would have 366 days. After adding 78 to the Śaka era year, if the sum is divisible by 4, then it would be a leap year. But when the sum becomes a multiple of 100, it would be a leap year only when it is divisible by 400; otherwise it would be a common year.
Caitra (or Chaitra as often written) should be the first month of the year and the lengths of the different months should be fixed as follows:— Caitra—30 days (31 days in a leap year).
Vaiśākha—31 days.
Jyeṣṭha—31 days.
Āṣāḍha—31 days.
Śrāvaṇa—31 days.
Bhādrapada—31 days.
Āśvina—30 days.
Kārttika—30 days.
Mārgaśīrṣa—30 days.
Pauṣa—30 days.
Māgha—30 days.
Phālguna—30 days.

The dates of the reformed Indian चलेन्दर् would thus have a permanent correspondence with the Gregorian चलेन्दर्. The corresponding dates would be:
Hindu Gregorian
Caitra 1 March 22 in a common year and 21 in a leap year.
Vaiṣākha 1 April 21.
Jyeṣṭha 1 May 22.
Āṣāḍha 1 June 22.
Śrāvaṇa 1 July 23.
Bhādrapada 1 August 23.
Āśvina 1 September 23.
Kārttika 1 October 23.
Mārgaśīrṣa 1 November 22.
Pauṣa 1 December 22.
Māgha 1 January 21.
Phālguna 1 February 20.

Unfortunately however, it did not gain popular acceptance due to the people being habituated to the old and traditional almanacs.

pañcaprāṇas
(‘the five vital-airs’)
------------------------------------------
See PRĀṆA.

pañcāyatanapūjā
(‘worship of five deities’)
------------------------------------------
The Ṛgveda (1.164.46) declares that ‘Sat’ or the Truth (= God, the Absolute) is one, but sages designate it by various names. Hence the various deities of the Hindu pantheon should be looked upon as various facets of one and the same God, generally called ब्रह्मन् or परमात्मन्, in the Hindu scriptures.
These deities can be classified into five groups, each group representing diffe-rent aspects of one principal god. They are: विष्णु, शिव, देवी, गणपति and सूर्य.
Gradually, various sects and cults grew round these deities. The votaries of these sects, forgetting the Ṛgvedic dictum and the philosophy of the one Supreme Being, became mutually exclusive or even hostile.
To rectify their attitude and put them back on the right track, शङ्कर (A.

pañcajana
(‘five [kinds or types of] people’)
------------------------------------------
This is one of the archaic words used in the वेदस्, the उपनिषद्स् and allied literature, whose interpretations vary widely.
In the Ṛgveda (10.53.4), this word forms a part of the मन्त्र to be chanted by the होतृ priest during the Darśapūrṇa-māsa sacrifice. Pañcajanas are the five types of persons to whom the होतृ priest is appealing to accept his duly discharged duties. They are: देवस् (gods); manuṣyas (human beings); पितृस् (manes); paśus (animals) and pakṣis (birds).
According to another interpretation they are the members of the four varṇas—brāhmaṇas, kṣattriyās, vaiśyas and śūdras—along with the niṣādas (hunters).
A third interpretation is that it refers to गन्धर्वस् (a kind of semigods), पितृस् (manes), देवस् (gods), असुरस् (antigods) and राक्षसस् (demons).
In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (

) this word has been used to indicate five kinds of beings who also are established in the आत्मन्/Brahman as their support. Here too, the interpretations given by the commentators are the same as the third and the second ones given above for the word in the Ṛgveda.
Pañcajana is also the name of a demon. See PĀÑCAJANYA for details.

Pañcabāṇa
(‘one who wields five arrows’)
------------------------------------------
Manmatha, the god of love or lust, is said to discharge five kinds of flowers as arrows from his bow made of sugarcane stalk towards his victims to make them lovelorn. Hence the name (pañca = five, बाण = arrow).
See also MANMATHA.

Pañcavaṭī
(‘a grove of five trees’)
------------------------------------------
During the last phase of his sojourn through the दण्डकारण्य forest, राम requested the sage अगस्त्य to suggest a good place in the forest where he could build a nice cottage and live like a recluse performing his duties. The sage in his reply (vide Araṇyakāṇḍa 13.13) suggested a place called पञ्चवटी near the गोदावरी river.
Rāma, along with सीता and लक्ष्मण, repaired to that place, built a beautiful cottage and started living there.
It was here that the lustful demoness शूर्पणखा was deformed by लक्ष्मण and the demons Khara and Dūṣaṇa along with their army were decimated by राम. Again, it was from here that सीता was abducted by the demon-king रावण.
It was called पञ्चवटी because it was a grove containing five (= pañca) banyan (= vaṭa) trees.
As per another view, the five specific trees are: अश्वत्थ (Ficus religiosa), बिल्व (Aegle marmelos), vaṭa (Ficus indica), dhātrī (Flacourtia cataphracta) and अशोक (Saraca indica).
According to one legend, five arrogant gandharva youths once surrounded the sage अगस्त्य and did not allow him to move about. He then cursed them to become trees. On their repentance and begging for pardon, he assured them of लिबेरतिओन् from that condition when राम would come and build his hermitage in their midst.
It has now been identified with a place near नासिक् (in Maharashtra) on the bank of the river गोदावरी.
Pañcavatī is also the name of a group of five big trees in Dakṣiṇeśvar (in Calcutta, now, Kolkata) under which the modern saint रामकृष्ण परमहṁस (A.
-1886), performed many auste-rities.

pañcamakāras
(‘five items [beginning with] the letter “ma”’)
------------------------------------------
See TANTRAS.

pañcabhūtas
(‘the five elements’)
------------------------------------------
See BHŪTA.

pañcācāras
(‘the five aspects of religious or spiritual conduct’)
------------------------------------------
These are the five religious disciplines prescribed for everyone of the Vīraśaiva sect.
See under ŚAIVISM.

Pañcānana
(‘the Five-faced One)
------------------------------------------
Comparable to the व्यूहस् or emanations of Lord विष्णु, is the पञ्चानन form of Lord शिव. पञ्चानन or the five-faced one represents the five aspects of शिव vis-a-vis the created universe. The five faces are respectively ईशान, Tatpuruṣa, अघोर, वामदेव and सद्योजात. The face ईशान turned towards the zenith, represents the highest aspect and is also called सदाशिव. On the physical plane, it represents the power that rules over ether or sky and on the spiritual plane, it is the deity that grants मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्. Tatpuruṣa facing east, stands for the power that rules over air and represents the forces of darkness and obscuration on the spiritual plane. अघोर, facing south and ruling over the element fire, stands for the power that absorbs and renovates the universe. वामदेव facing north, ruling over the element water, is responsible for preservation. सद्योजात, facing west represents the power that creates.
Iconographical works describe पञ्चानन (Śiva) as five-faced and ten-armed. He has fifteen eyes. Seated on a bull he wears an elephant’s hide round his waist and a tiger’s skin as the upper garment. He has an immense body and matted hair dressed up as a tall crown. He holds in his hands the following objects: शक्ति (a weapon), खट्वाङ्ग (a magical wand), त्रिशूल (trident), अक्षमाला (rosary), abhayamudrā (gesture of protection), varadamudrā (gesture of bestowal of boons), a fruit, a snake, डमरु (hand-drum) and utpala flower.
Sinners can get their sins absolved by worshipping this aspect of शिव.

pañcadaśākṣarī-mantra
(‘mantra of fifteen letters or syllables’)
------------------------------------------
This is a fifteen-lettered (pañcadaśa = fifteen) मन्त्र or mystic formula closely associated with the goddess ललिता त्रिपुर-sundarī (an aspect of पार्वती) and her emblem, the श्रीचक्र.
Actually there are two such mantras: the one attributed to the sage अगस्त्य which begins with the letter ‘ka’ (hence the name kādimata) and another to his wife लोपामुद्रा which begins with the letter ‘ha’ (hence the name hādimata).
The मन्त्र has to be received ceremonially from a competent गुरु.
It is said to be a very powerful मन्त्र.
See also LALITĀ, ŚRĪCAKRA and TANTRAS.

pañcāṅgaśuddhi
(‘holy period according to the पञ्चाङ्ग or almanac’)
------------------------------------------
Any auspicious rite should be performed when all the five aspects dealt with in a पञ्चाङ्ग (Hindu almanac) are deemed as auspicious. This is पञ्चाङ्ग-शुद्धि.
These five aspects have been dealt with in detail in PAÑCĀṄGA.

Pañcatantra
(‘five rules of political conduct’)
------------------------------------------
The Pañcatantra is the most celebrated and interesting work in Sanskrit literature, classed under the didactic fable group. It comprises five books or sections (pañca = five), each dealing with one par-ticular tantra or rule of political conduct.
The introductory part of the work states that it was taught by a wise teacher, Viṣṇuśarma by name, to the idle and stupid sons of a king Amaraśakti of Mahilaropa, at his request. The princes very soon became well-educated and well-behaved, due to the marvellous effect of the tales they heard from their preceptor.
Till now, the identity of neither the teacher nor the king has been determined.
The earliest edition known to us—though completely lost—is the Pehlevi (language) translation by a Persian physi-cian Burzoe, at the order of the king Khossu Anushirvan (A.
-575). The text we now have is based on an old Syrian version by Bud in A.
and an Arabic version by Abdallah Ibnal Mogaffa in A.
. This latter work was translated into several European languages during the period A.

to 1678.
The Pañcatantra is generally assigned to the period 100 B. C. to A.

.
The contents of the work may be summarised as follows:
1. Mitrabheda
(Breaking the Friendship)
This deals with the policy of ‘divide and rule’ by the story of two jackals, Karaṭaka and Damanaka, who lived happily after estranging the lion and the bull who had been fast friends for a long time.
2. Mitralābha
(Acquisition of Friends)
This illustrates the advantages of a judicious friendship by the story of the adventures of a tortoise, a deer, a crow and a mouse.
3. Kākolukīya
(Tale of Crows and Owls)
This brings out the dangers of friendship between those who are natural enemies.
4. Labdhapraṇāśa
(Loss of what has been Acquired)
This points out, by means of the story of an ape and a crocodile, how certain weaknesses lead to the loss of one’s own possessions.
5. Aparīkṣitakāritam
(Results of Inconsiderate Actions)
The general principle of ‘haste makes waste’ is illustrated through a number of stories here.
There are two distinct versions of the Pañcatantra available now: the Tantrā-khyāyikā (Kashmir version) in simple prose; the stories found in the Kathā-saritsāgara of Somadeva and the Bṛhatkathāmañjarī of Kṣemendra.
The Pañcatantra is one of the most translated works in world literature.
See also HITOPADEŚA.

Pañcaviṁśa Brāhmaṇa
------------------------------------------
The Tāṇḍya Mahābrāhmaṇa of the Sāmaveda is known by this name since it has pañcaviṁśa or twenty-five chapters.
See TĀṆḌYA MAHĀBRĀHMAṆA for details.

pañcamahāyajñas
(‘five great sacrifices’)
------------------------------------------
Though the Hindu scriptures have eulogised सṁन्यास (the life of a monk, a man of total renunciation and dedication to God) they have also boldly declared that the गृहस्थ is the pivot of the whole society since the members of all the other three āśramas depend upon him for their sustenance.
The life of a householder is itself a यज्ञ or a sacrifice, for the good of the whole society. As if to remind him of this, he has been ordained to perform everyday, five yajñas. These are collectively called ‘pañcamahāyajñas’. They are: देवयज्ञ, पितृयज्ञ, ऋषियज्ञ, nṛyajña and भूत-यज्ञ.
Devayajña or sacrifice to gods like सूर्य, प्रजापति and इन्द्र, is the usual daily sacrifice offered in a consecrated fire. Since they give us rain, crops and prosperity they have to be satiated through these oblations.
Pitṛyajña or sacrifice to the manes (the forefathers) consists in offering rice balls (called पिण्ड) and water (arghya). By this offering they are satisfied and bless their descendants who are performing this sacrifice.
Ṛṣiyajña (also called ब्रह्मयज्ञ, ‘brahma’ meaning the वेदस्) is sacrifice to the ṛṣis or the sages. Since they have transmitted the knowledge of the वेदस् to mankind, it is the householder’s duty to recite the वेदस् and also teach them to his children and disciples. This itself is the यज्ञ by which they are pleased.
Nṛyajña and भूतयज्ञ are actually feeding hungry human beings that may visit the होउसे as also the domestic and other animals.
By performing these five daily sacrifices, the householder is actually repaying his debts to the divine beings and the society, from whom he has received help and sustenance. They also help him in offsetting the sin he commits (unknowingly and unwillingly) while using the five implements in his होउसे like the pestle and mortar, domestic fire, grinding stone etc., wherein violence is perpetrated on life through the killing of ants, worms and so on.

pañcabhedas
(‘five kinds of [fundamental] differences’)
------------------------------------------
See DVAITA VEDĀNTA DARŚANA.

pañcīkaraṇa
(‘the process of quintuplication’)
------------------------------------------
This is a technical term specially found in the treatises on Advaita Vedānta.
The process by which each of the pañcamahābhūtas (five great elements) is formed out of the pañcatanmātras (five primordial elements) is called ‘pañcī-karaṇa’. Each former element—because of this—contains half of the corresponding tanmātra and one-eighth of each of the other four. For instance, one unit of the mahābhūta पृथ्वी = 1/2 पृथ्वी tanmātra + 1/8 of ap tanmātra + 1/8 of अग्नि tanmātra + 1/8 of वायु tanmātra + 1/8 of आकाश tanmātra. Because of this पञ्चीकरण, each of the महाभूतस् contains a part of the other four bhūtas and hence their characteristics.

pañcagavya
(‘five products [derived] from a cow’)
------------------------------------------
The Hindu society has been venerating the cow for over three millennia. Working for the good of ‘go-ब्राह्मण,’ the cows and the ब्राह्मणस्, has been considered as a very pious act.
The Hindu धर्मशास्त्रस् have prescribed several prāyaścittas or expiations for sins. In many of these rites consuming the पञ्चगव्य finds a place, thereby reflecting the great veneration for the cow.
The पञ्चगव्य is a preparation from five (= pañca) products derived from a cow (= gavya). They are: milk, curds, ghee, urine and dung. The proportion in which they are mixed is 8:8:4:2:1
All these are to be taken from a kapilā (brown) cow. While preparing it, several mantras from the Ṛgveda (for e.g., 1.91.16; 4.39.6) and other वेदस् (for e.g., Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.1; Vājasaneyī Saṁhitā 22.1) are to be chanted. A part of it, mixed with green दर्भ (Poa cynosuroides) is offered into fire with some more Vedic mantras and the remainder is consumed with a special मन्त्र indicating the power of this पञ्चगव्य to burn up all sins.

Pañcanada
(‘the [land of] five rivers’)
------------------------------------------
The country Madradeśa or Araṭṭa was called पञ्चनद (pañca = five; nada = river) since the Sindhū (Indus river) and its five tributaries—Śatadrū (Sutlej), विपाशा (Beas), Irāvatī (Rāvi), चन्द्रभागा (Chenab) and वितस्ता (Jhelum)—flowed through it. It roughly corresponds to the modern Punjab (of both India and Pakistan).
A demon Jalandhara had his capital here (the modern Jalandhar). He was later killed by Lord शिव.
One of the 51 शक्तिपीठस् (places sacred to the Divine मोथेर्) is situated here. The temple of Viśvamukhi houses the goddess.

pañcatapas
(‘austerity involving ड़िवे ड़िरेस्’)
------------------------------------------
Tapas or austerity ia a must before embarking on any important venture or even for self-purification.
One such तपस् is पञ्चतपस् or pañcāgnitapas. In this mode of austerity, the aspirant is to sit in the midst of four blazing agnis or fires in an open place, with the sun burning above his head as the fifth fire. He has to sit in their midst from dawn to dusk, for a specified period, after preparing himself ceremonially as per the prescribed rules.
According to some, this is a substitute for the performance of वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्, while maintaining the duly consecrated Vedic fires.
Śrī Sāradā देवी (A.
-1920) the consort of रामकृष्ण परमहṁस (A.
-1886) is known to have performed this तपस् in A.

Pañcāgnividyā
(‘the doctrine of the ड़िवे ड़िरेस्’)
------------------------------------------
See VIDYĀS.

pañcamas
(‘[those who belong to] the fifth [caste]’)
------------------------------------------
The four varṇas (or castes) into which the Hindu society was (and is) divided is well-known. Certain castes which were considered as outside this category, were relegated to the ‘fifth’ (= pañcama) place.
Almost all those who have been listed among the Scheduled Castes and Tribes in modern India come under this category.
See CASTE SYSTEM.

pañcopacāras
(‘the five उपचारस् or modes of service’)
------------------------------------------
In पूजा or ritualistic worship of a deity, the उपचारस् or direct modes of offering are important. They may generally be five or ten or sixteen.
When they are five, they are called ‘pañcopacāras’ (pañca = five).
They are: गन्ध (sandal-paste); puṣpa (flowers along with बिल्व and तुलसी leaves as also dūrva or grass); धूप (incense); dīpa (lighted lamp for waving before the deity) and naivedya (food-offering).
See also DEVAPŪJĀ.

pañcākṣarī
(‘[a मन्त्र of] five syllables’)
------------------------------------------
Meditation on the form of the इष्टदेवता (chosen deity) as also the जप or repetition of the मन्त्र (divine name or formula) connected with that deity is an important and integral part of sādhana or spiritual practice.
Out of the several modes of designating a मन्त्र, the one that indicates the number of syllables is quite common. Thus ekākṣarī, पञ्चाक्षरी, षडक्षरी, अष्टाक्षरी, navākṣarī and dvādaśākṣarī represent the mantras having one, five, six, eight, nine or twelve syllables.
However, some of these general terms, due to constant usage, get particularised. For instance, the pañcā-kṣarī refers to the five-syllabled मन्त्र of शिव only, viz., namaś-śivāya (= na-maś-śi-vā-ya) (Hence it is called Śivapañcākṣarī.)
Similarly the अष्टाक्षरी refers to the famous मन्त्र of Nārāyaṇa—oṁ namo nārāyaṇāya.
By adding the letter Oṁ to the five-syllabled मन्त्र of शिव, we get the षडक्षरी (= six-lettered) मन्त्र. Both these mantras of शिव are well-known and are widely used for जप or repetition.
Since Oṁ is often an integral part of most mantras (almost considered as a must), even the six-syllabled मन्त्र is considered as पञ्चाक्षरी only.
It was originally discovered by the sage वामदेव and the छन्दस् (metre) of revelation is the Vedic paṅkti. सदाशिव is the deity.
The works on the mantras, like the तन्त्रस् and पुराणस्, give the processes of purification of oneself like अङ्गन्यास (of limbs), करन्यास (of the hands) and so on as also the dhyānaśloka, giving the details for meditation on the form of the deity.
This मन्त्र can be repeated for the sake of मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन् through self-purification. However it can also be repeated to get one’s desires fulfilled, such as long life, freedom from diseases as also the troubles created by evil forces, and so on.
Such जप or repetition may run into lakhs and has to be practised in places like the top of a hillock, the bank of a river or some such holy place (of solitude). It must then be followed by होम (offering special oblations into a duly consecrated fire), the number of oblations generally being one-tenth of the number of जप.
This पञ्चाक्षरी मन्त्र has been highly eulogised in Śaivite works.

pañcayajñas
(‘the five [daily] sacrifices’)
------------------------------------------
See PAÑCAMAHĀYAJÑAS.

pañcopāsakas
(‘five classes of worshippers’)
------------------------------------------
Hindus can generally be classed into three groups: śaivas (worshippers of शिव); śāktas (worshippers of शक्ति or the देवी, the Divine मोथेर्) and vaiṣṇavas (worshippers of विष्णु).
Śaṅkara (A.

-820) during his days, attempted to unite the various mutually warring sects by introducing the practice of pañcadevatāpūjā or pañco-pāsanā. Here he has added two more deities: गणपति and सूर्य. The worshippers of these are called गाणपत्यस् and Sauras.
This takes the number of the sects to five.
These five classes of worshippers together are called ‘pañcopāsakas’ (pañca = five; upāsaka = worshipper).

Pañcaśikha
(‘one with five locks of hair [on the head]’)
------------------------------------------
One of the six systems of Hindu philosophy whose elements are rooted in the Vedic literature, and, which is extant even today as an important subject of study is the साङ्ख्य दर्शन. This system is said to have been originally taught by the sage कपिल and further expounded and expanded by his disciple आसुरि as also his student पञ्चशिख.
One पञ्चशिख is mentioned by the महाभारत (Śāntiparva, 219) as a teacher of the king जनक.
He is said to have authored a voluminous work, Ṣaṣṭitantra (in sixty chapters, in two parts, containing thirty two and twenty-eight chapters each) which is not available now. This name might have been given to that work since it was said to deal with sixty (= ṣaṣṭi) topics of Sāṅkhya philosophy.
Twenty-one sūtras in prose have been quoted in the Vyāsabhāṣya on the Yoga-sūtras of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) as of पञ्चशिख.
He might have lived during the first century B. C.
His Sāṅkhya probably represents a transitional stage from that of the उपनिषद्स् to that propounded by ईश्वर-कृष्ण (A.
) in his Sāṅkhyakārikā.

Pañcadaśī
(‘[a work of] fifteen [chapters]’)
------------------------------------------
All the three major schools of Vedānta—Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita, and Dvaita—though based on the प्रस्थानत्रय (the three basic works), also have special treatises called ‘Prakaraṇagranthas’ which can be termed as textbooks of those schools.
The Pañcadaśī of विद्यारण्य मुनि (14th century A. D.) who was the pontiff of the Śāradā-मठ of Śṛṅgerī (in the present Karnataka State) from A.

to 1386, is one such work of the Advaita school. It is a voluminous work of 1571 verses spread out in fifteen chapters (hence the name Pañcadaśī, pañcadaśa meaning fifteen).
These fifteen chapters have been grouped into three pentads: Vivekapañcaka (dealing with the discrimination of the real from the unreal); Dīpapañcaka (expounding the nature of the Self as pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्) and Ānandapañcaka (dwelling on the bliss-nature of ब्रह्मन्).
These three pentads have for their theme, the three aspects of ब्रह्मन्, viz., sat, cit and आनन्द.
It is an elegant work written in a simple style, though dealing with a tough subject.
There is only one Sanskrit commentary, Tātparyadīpikā, by रामकृष्ण about whom nothing is known.
A brief account of the contents of this treatise may now be given:
Chapter 1 (Tattvaviveka; 65 verses)
This chapter deals with the nature of the आत्मन् (the Self), प्रकृति (Mother Nature), the five bhūtas (elements like the earth and water), पञ्चीकरण (quintuplication of the elements), the pañca-kośas (five sheaths) and the meaning of the mahāvākya tat tvam asi.
Chapter 2 (Pañcamahābhūtaviveka; 109 verses)
Apart from a detailed treatment of the five fundamental elements and their products, this section also deals with the nature of māyā, its characteristics and effects.
Chapter 3 (Pañcakośaviveka; 43 verses)
The पञ्चकोशस् or the five sheaths (like the annamayakośa or the sheath of ड़ोओद्) that cover the nature of the आत्मन्, and the real nature of the आत्मन् as sat-cit-आनन्द (existence-चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्-bliss) as also the ultimate identity of the jīvātman (the individual सोउल्) with ब्रह्मन् (the Supreme सोउल् or the Absolute) are the topics discussed here.
Chapter 4 (Dvaitaviveka; 69 verses)
Creation of the world by ईश्वर (God), the relation of the जीव (individual सोउल्) with ईश्वर as also the world, division of द्वैत (consciousness of duality) into two varieties, what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted—these are the subjects dealt with in this chapter.
Chapter 5 (Mahāvākyaviveka; 8 verses)
This short chapter delineates the method of interpreting the four mahā-vākyas or ‘great sentences’ taken from the उपनिषद्स्.
Chapter 6 (Citradīpa; 290 Verses)
If the first five chapters of this work contained the suffix ‘viveka’ in their titles—because they dealt with विवेक or various types of discrimination that help in understanding the principles of the Advaita school better—the five chapters from the 6th to the 10th, containing the suffix ‘dīpa’ (= light or lamp) throw light on the subtler aspects of the same school.
In this chapter which is quite exhaustive, comparison is made between the various stages of a citra (drawing or painting) and the degrees of manifestation of परमात्मन् (the Supreme Self) as cit (pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्), अन्तर्यामिन् (the inner controller) and so on.
Chapter 7 (Tṛptidīpa;298 verses)
This also is a long chapter. Whatever tṛpti or satisfaction a being gets in any experience, is due to the presence of the आत्मन् (Self) only. However, infinite tṛpti can be got only through the knowledge of ब्रह्मन्.
Chapter 8 (Kūṭasthadīpa; 73 verses)
The word ‘kūṭastha’ refers to the undifferentiated, pure, चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. Just as general sunlight lights up a wall whereas the same, reflected from a mirror, appears brighter, in the same way, the kūṭastha lights up both the outside world and the बुद्धि or the intellect. Ultimately, it is different from both the outside world and the जीव inside, who is only a reflection of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. However, it should be known that this kūṭastha and ब्रह्मन् are one and the same.
Chapter 9 (Dhyānadīpa; 158 verses)
This chapter states that upāsanā or meditation on the knowledge gained through a correct understanding of the scriptures, though indirect, can also lead to मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्. Incidentally, the forms of God such as विष्णु and so on, are accepted as real for the purpose of meditation since they are sanctioned by the scriptures.
Chapter 10 (Nāṭakadīpa; 26 verses)
The lamp (= dīpa) in a dancing hall or the stage of a theatre, lights up everything, by its mere presence. But it is not affected in any way by the happenings on the stage. Similarly the real Self, the आत्मन्, called ‘sākṣicaitanya’ or ‘witness-चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्’, also reveals all the activities of the body-मिन्द् complex without itself undergoing any change. This is the gist of this chapter.
Chapter 11 (Yogānanda; 134 verses)
The spiritual felicity arising out of the realisation of ब्रह्मन् is the subject-matter of the five chapters 11 to 15. Hence the use of the word ‘ānanda’ in the titles.
There is an experience of आनन्द or bliss in the सुषुप्ति or deep-sleep state. This also is an aspect of the bliss of ब्रह्मन्. Far greater is the degree of such bliss in the समाधि or superconscious state. This is the gist of this chapter.
Chapter 12 (Ātmānanda; 90 verses)
The concept that everyone loves or likes another person or object is for his own sake—as described by the sage Yājña-valkya in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (4.5.6)—is expounded here.
Chapter 13 (Advaitānanda; 105 verses)
Brahman is आनन्द or bliss. Jagat or the world is an apparent product of that ब्रह्मन् and hence is identical with It. The शक्ति (power) or māyā which produces this world-appearance in ब्रह्मन् cannot be defined. When this world is ignored as असत् (unreal), its true nature as ब्रह्मन् is realised.
To put it in another way, when nāma (names) and rūpa (forms) are considered as important, ब्रह्मन् appears as a real jagat. When they are ignored and only the basic stuff is noticed, ब्रह्मन् as sat-cit-आनन्द is experienced.
Chapter 14 (Vidyānanda; 65 verses)
Vidyānanda is the bliss got out of the knowledge of ब्रह्मन्. It has four aspects: absence of sorrow; attainment of all desires; the feeling that one has fulfilled all the duties of life; the sense of having achieved all that is to be achieved in life. This is the essence of this chapter.

Pañcabhūtaliṅgas
(‘Śivaliṅgas connected with the five bhūtas or elements’)
------------------------------------------
Pañcabhūtas are the five fundamental elements out of which the whole material world is created. They are: पृथ्वी (earth); ap (water); तेजस् (fire); वायु (air); आकाश (space or ether).
The Śivaliṅgas in some well-known places of पिल्ग्रिमगे are said to be closely associated with these five. They are:
Pṛthvīliṅga at Kāñcīpuram (in Tamil Nadu)
Abliṅga at Jambukeśvara (in Tamil Nadu)
Tejoliṅga at Aruṇācala (in Tamil Nadu)
Vāyuliṅga at Kāḷahasti (in Andhra Pradesh)
Ākāśaliṅga at Cidambaram (in Tamil Nadu).

The exact reason for such classification is not known.

Pañcakośas
(‘five sheaths’)
------------------------------------------
According to the Vedānta philosophy, the true nature of the human being—for that matter, any living being or even the whole creation—is आत्मन्, the Self. Though this आत्मन् is ever present in us, we do not feel its presence. On the other hand, we identify ourselves with the body and मिन्द्, and hence, suffer. The factors responsible for this hiding or covering of our true nature are five: the physical body which is a product of अन्न or ड़ोओद्, प्राण or the vital energies responsible for the functioning of the sense-organs as also other biochemical processes within the body, मनस् or the मिन्द्, विज्ञान or the intellect, also called बुद्धि, and अज्ञान or basic इग्नोरन्चे. These five are respectively called अन्नमय-कोश, prāṇamaya-कोश, manomaya-कोश, vijñānamaya-कोश and ānandamaya-कोश. कोश means a sheath. Since these factors cover the आत्मन् like a sheath and are five in number, they are called पञ्चकोशस्.
Annamaya-कोश the first, consists of the physical body given by the parents and nourished by अन्न or ड़ोओद्. The five prāṇas or vital energies like प्राण, अपान and others form the second, the प्राणमयकोश. मनस् or the मिन्द् with its capacity for चोग्नितिओन्, will and doubts comprises the third, the manomaya-कोश. विज्ञान or the intellect, with its capacity to weigh the pros and cons, and come to definite conclusions is the fourth, the vijñānamayakośa. आनन्दमयकोश the fifth, is the name given to अज्ञान or इग्नोरन्चे. The आनन्द or happiness that is enjoyed during deep-sleep is due to it. Hence the name.
Annamayakośa is the outermost cover. प्राणमयकोश is within it, filling it fully and of the same form. So also manomaya, vijñānamaya and ānandamaya kośas which succeed prānamayakośa in that order, fill their preceding kośas.
By a process of negation, negating each of these kośas as not-self, one can arrive at the true Self.

Pāñcajanya
(‘[the conch’] derived from पञ्चजन’)
------------------------------------------
In the olden days, a शङ्ख or a conch was as much an appendage for the क्षत्त्रिय warriors as it was for the ब्राह्मणस् in their ritualistic worship. It was used, like a horn, to blow, signifying a challenge for a fight, the beginning and the end of a battle (every day) and so on.
Famous warriors usually gave special names to their weapons and śaṅkhas. कृष्ण’s शङ्ख was known as पाञ्चजन्य, युधिष्ठिर’s as Anantavijaya, अर्जुन’s as Devadatta and भीम’s as Pauṇḍra.
Pañcajana was a fierce demon who lived in a miniscule form inside a शङ्ख at the bottom of the sea. Once he abducted the only son of the sage सान्दीपनि and ate him up.
After completing their एदुचतिओन् under सान्दीपनि, when कृष्ण and बलराम requested him to accept their गुरुदक्षिणा (honorarium paid generally at the end of एदुचतिओन्) he expressed a desire to get back his lost son.
Coming to know all the details regarding the boy’s disappearance, कृष्ण and बलराम dived into the sea, killed the demon पञ्चजन, usurped the शङ्ख in which he was dwelling and later got the boy back from यमलोक, the world of यम (the god of death).
Since this शङ्ख was obtained from पञ्चजन, it was named पाञ्चजन्य.
Pāñcajanya was also the name of a forest near the Raivataka mountain.

pañcatattvas
(‘five basic principles’)
------------------------------------------
They are the same as the ‘pañcama-kāras’. See TANTRAS.
They may also be the five elements—also called ‘pañcabhūtas’—viz., पृथ्वी (earth), ap (water), तेजस् (fire), वायु (air) and आकाश (ether).

Pāñcarātra Āgamas
(‘āgamas belonging to the Pāñcarātra school’)
------------------------------------------
Introduction
Āgamas are a special class of Hindu religio-philosophical literature handed down through a succession of teachers from the most ancient days.
Whether they represented a system parallel to and separate from the Vedic traditions or a continuation of the same and rooted in them, has been a subject of discussion among the scholars.
However, यामुनाचार्य (A.

-1038) in his scholarly work, the Āgama-prāmāṇya, has conclusively established their affinity with the वेदस्.
Of the three kinds of āgamas—the Śaiva, the शाक्त (or the tantra) and the Vaiṣṇava—the Pāñcarātra Āgamas belong to the last group.
The other branch of the Vaiṣṇavāgamas is the Vaikhānasa Āgama or the Vaikhānasa Sūtras.
Derivation of the Name
The literal meaning of the word ‘Pāñcarātra’ means ‘that which is connected with five nights’.
Lord Keśava (Viṣṇu or नारायण) is said to have taught this esoteric science to अनन्त, गरुड, विष्वक्सेन, ब्रह्मा and रुद्र, over five nights (pañca = five; rātra = night).
The word rātra also means ज्ञान, knowledge or wisdom. Since it teaches five kinds of knowledge it is called Pāñcarātra. These are: tattva (cosmology); muktiprada (that which gives मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन्); bhaktiprada (that which confers devotion); yaugika (yoga); vaiṣayika (objects of desire).
Or, alternatively, since it teaches about the five aspects of God (called पुरुषोत्तम) viz., पर (highest), vyūha (emanation), विभव (an इन्चर्नतिओन्), अन्तर्यामिन् (indweller) and अर्चा (form for worship), it is called ‘Pāñcarātra’.
Pāñcarātra Literature
The Pāñcarātra literature is very vast, The total number of works—generally called ‘saṁhitā’ or ‘tantra’—exceeds two hundred, as per the lists given in various works, though only a few have been printed. Quite a few are in the form of manuscripts preserved in oriental libra-ries. Many others are not available in any form though their names are mentioned in other works.
The following is a list of the works as available now, along with a very brief summary of each.
1. Ahirbudhnya Saṁhitā
This is a fairly voluminous work with 3880 verses in 60 chapters. The speciality of this work is that it deals with the four व्यूहस् or emanations of the Lord, description of several mantras (sacred syllables) and yantras (magical diagrams) as also rituals for curing diseases. (See AHIRBUDHNYA SAṀHITĀ for details.)
2. अनिरुद्ध Saṁhitā
Also called Aniruddhasaṁhitā-mahopaniṣad, it has 34 chapters dealing entirely with the descriptions of various rituals, methods of initiation, prāyaścittas or expiations for sins, rules for making and installing the images of gods and other similar topics.
3. Hayaśīrṣa Saṁhitā
A fairly exhaustive work in 144 chapters, distributed among four Kāṇḍas or sections—Pratiṣṭhākāṇḍa, Saṅkarṣaṇa-kāṇḍa, Liṅgakāṇḍa and Saurakāṇḍa—it deals primarily with the rituals concerning the installation of images of various minor deities as also the methods of preparing them.
4. ईश्वर Saṁhitā
It is a work of 24 chapters of which sixteen deal with ritualistic worship. Other subjects treated in this work are: description of images, methods of दीक्षा or spiritual initiation, practice of meditation, details regarding mantras, methods of self-control and the greatness of the Yādava Hill (now known as ‘Melkoṭe’, a Vaiṣṇava pilgrim centre on a hillock near Mysore, Karnataka State).
5. Jayākhya Saṁhitā
This work is one of the three cardinal texts of the Pāñcarātra literature. It has thirty-three paṭalas or chapters and deals with the following topics: detailed account of च्रेअतिओन्; yogābhyāsa (practice of योग) and mantropāsanā (spiritual practice through the repetition of mantras or sacred formulae); various Vaiṣṇava mantras; पूजा (ritualistic worship) and होम (fire ritual); दीक्षा (initiation); temples and worship therein; ācāras (the codes of conduct) for the vaiṣṇavas; and, prāyaścittas or expiations for sins.
6. Kāśyapa Saṁhitā
This is a comparatively small work in twelve chapters. It deals mainly with poisons and methods of remedy by suitable mantras or incantations.
7. Mahā-sanatkumāra Saṁhitā
This is a voluminous work of ten thousand verses spread over forty sections in four chapters. It deals entirely with rituals of worship.
8. Pādma Saṁhitā
A work dealing mainly with rituals and chanting of mantras, this work is in thirty-one chapters.
9. Parama Saṁhitā
A work in thirty-one chapters, it deals with the following topics: process of च्रेअतिओन्; rituals of initiation and worship; योग classified as ज्ञानयोग and कर्मयोग.
It declares that ज्ञानयोग which includes प्राणायाम and समाधि is superior to कर्मयोग. कर्मयोग seems to mean ritualistic worship of विष्णु.
10. Pārameśvara Saṁhitā
A short work in fifteen chapters, it deals with meditation on mantras, sacrifices and methods of rituals as also prāyaścittas or expiations.
11. पराशर Saṁhitā
A concise work in eight chapters, it deals with the methods of जप or the muttering of the name of

God.
12

. Pauṣkara Saṁhitā
Considered as one of the earliest works of the Pāñcarātra system, the Pauṣkara Saṁhitā consists of forty-three chapters. Apart from dealing with various kinds of image-worship, it also contains certain philosophical views. It is interesting to note that some funeral sacrifices also find a place here.
13. सुदर्शन Saṁhitā
A treatise comprising forty-one chapters, it deals mainly with meditation on mantras and expiations for sins.
14. Vihagendra Saṁhitā
It is in twenty-four chapters. Apart from meditation on mantras, it deals with sacrificial oblations. In the twelfth chapter, the topic of प्राणायाम, as a part of the process of worship, is also described extensively.
15. विष्णु Saṁhitā
A work in thirty chapters, it also deals mainly with ritualistic worship. Its philosophy is akin to that of साङ्ख्य दर्शन with some variations like the पुरुष (the individual सोउल्) being all-pervading and that he activates the प्रकृति to evolve into the world.
16. Viṣṇutattva Saṁhitā
Comprising thirty-nine chapters, it deals with image-worship, ablutions and wearing of the vaiṣṇava marks and some purificatory rites.
Philosophy of the Pāñcarātra Āgamas
The philosophy of this system has been expounded in the Jayākhya Saṁhitā in detail. A brief summary of the same will be given here.
Though यज्ञ (Vedic sacrifices), दान (giving gifts), स्वाध्याय (study of the वेदस्) and other similar religious disciplines are useful in spiritual life, it is only ज्ञान (knowledge) of the paratattva or the Highest Reality that can really give मोक्ष.
This paratattva (God) is the same as the ब्रह्मन् of the वेदस् and the उपनिषद्स्. He is of the nature of pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् (cit) and bliss (ānanda). He is anādi and अनन्त (without beginning or end). He is the substratum and support of the whole universe. Though he is beyond all guṇas, he is also the भोक्तृ (experiencer, enjoyer) of all that is born out of the guṇas. He is sarvajña (omniscient) and sarvaśakta (omnipotent). He is both transcendent and immanent with regard to this created universe. Hence he is too subtle to be perceived by the senses or the मिन्द्. However he can be realised through the pure मिन्द्. This is called ‘mānasika-प्रत्यक्ष’.
The Jīvas, when they realise this ब्रह्मन् or God, appear to have become one with him, but do maintain a subtle distinction also from him. Hence this philosophy can be called ‘bhedābheda’ or ‘dvaitādvaita’.
As regards सृष्टि or च्रेअतिओन्, three kinds of it are recognised: Brahmasarga, Prakṛtisarga and Śuddhasarga.
Brahmasarga is the projection of the four-faced ब्रह्मा from विष्णु and the च्रेअतिओन् of the world by ब्रह्मा.
Prakṛtisarga is similar to the च्रेअतिओन् as described in the Sāṅkhya philosophy. प्रकृति or प्रधान comprises the three well-known guṇas—sattva, रजस् and तमस्.
The first product of the evolution of प्रधान when सत्त्व is predominant, is बुद्धि (cosmic intellect). The second product when रजस् has gained the upper hand, is अहङ्कार (egoism). This is of three types: prakāśātma or taijasātma; vikṛtātma; bhūtātma. The first gives rise to the five ज्ञानेन्द्रियस् (organs of know-ledge) and the मिन्द्. The second produces the five कर्मेन्द्रियस् (organs of action). From the last evolve the sūkṣmabhūtas or तन्मात्रस् (the five subtle elements). These then create the five gross elements. The whole च्रेअतिओन् comes out of a combi-nation of these basic products.
The puruṣas or jīvas (souls) get associated with the bodies in accordance with their कर्म, due to the will of God. Their association with the inert bodies makes the latter appear as conscious even as an iron piece acts like a magnet in the vicinity of a powerful magnet.
The Śuddhasarga is the third च्रेअतिओन्. Here, God—called पुरुषोत्तम Vāsudeva—evolves from out of himself three subsidiary agents or forms: Acyuta, सत्य and पुरुष. These forms in reality are non-different from him. The third form—Puruṣa—acts as the अन्तर्यामिन् or the inner controller. It is he who inspires all the gods to work. It is he who binds the jīvas with vāsanās (residual impressions) and again, it is he who inspires them to do sādhanas (spiritual disciplines) to get out of the bondage of vāsanās.
The māyā (delusion) power of God makes the jīvas (through vāsanās or past impressions) get identified with the body-मिन्द् complex. This association of the vāsanās is anādi or beginningless. However, by the grace of God, the अन्तर्यामिन् or the indwelling power and spirit, the जीव awakens to true knowledge and gets liberated from all the shackles.
The path to this मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन् starts with the inspiration by God for the जीव to search out a great गुरु or spiritual preceptor. This गुरु gives the disciple mantradīkṣā (initiation with a holy name or syllable). Regular and steady practice of the mantrajapa (repetition of the divine name) results in समाधि or total absorption in God.
The upāsanā or meditation on God has two stages. The first is called ‘kriyākhya’. It is in the form of practising various virtues like शौच (cleanliness), यज्ञ (sacrifices), तपस् (austerity), अध्ययन (studying the scriptures), अहिṁसा (not harming others), सत्य (truth), karuṇā (compassion), दान (giving gifts) and so on.
The second is called ‘sattākhya’ or ‘jñānākhya’. It is practically the same as ज्ञानयोग. The मिन्द् purified by the practice of kriyākhya is now able to meditate on the आत्मन् inside, which results in the experience of unitive चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् that jñātṛ (knower), jñeya (object to be known) and ज्ञान (knowledge) are all one and the same.
The Pāñcarātra Āgamas—especially the Jayākhya Saṁhitā—describe two types of yogas: mantradhyāna and yogābhyāsa.
The former consists of meditation on God with form along with the repetition of appropriate mantras. The latter is almost the same as the योग of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.).
A special contribution of the Pāñca-rātra Āgamas to the religio-philosophical literature of हिन्दुइस्म् is the concept of the व्यूहस् which are four. (Hence the name ‘Caturvyūhas,’ ‘catur’ meaning ‘four’.)
‘Vyūha’ means a projection or an emanation.
In this system, the various names by which God the Supreme is known are: परमात्मन्, नारायण, विष्णु, भगवान् and वासुदेव.
‘Bhaga’ means ṣaḍguṇas or the group of six blessed qualities. They are: ज्ञान (knowledge); ऐश्वर्य (lordship); शक्ति (ability, potency); बल (strength); vīrya (virility, unaffectedness) and तेजस् (splendour).
Since God—more commonly known as वासुदेव in this system—has all these guṇas or attributes in the fullest measure, he is called ‘Bhagavān’.
By the will of भगवान् वासुदेव (the first or the original Vyūha) the second Vyūha, सङ्कर्षण (or बलराम) emerges. From सङ्कर्षण emanates प्रद्युम्न and from him, अनिरुद्ध.
Though the latter three व्यूहस् are also, in essence, equal to वासुदेव, they manifest only two of the six guṇas prominently, the other four being in a latent condition.
If in सङ्कर्षण, ज्ञान and बल are predominant, प्रद्युम्न manifests ऐश्वर्य and vīrya more prominently. अनिरुद्ध, on the other hand, exhibits शक्ति and तेजस् to a much greater degree.
Each of the व्यूहस् is credited with two activities, a creative and a moral one.
Each of the व्यूहस्, again, gives rise to three more sub-व्यूहस्, making a total of twelve emanations. They are: Keśava, नारायण, Mādhava, Govinda, विष्णु, Madhusūdana, त्रिविक्रम, वामन, Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha and Dāmodara.
These twelve are considered as the māsādhipas or the adhidevatās (tutelary deities) of the twelve lunar months. They are also offered अर्घ्य (ceremonial water) in ritualistic worship.
Iconographically, all of them are identical except for the arrangement of the four emblems of Viṣṇu—śaṅkha (conch), चक्र (discus), गदा (mace) and पद्म (lotus)—in the four hands.
Conclusion
The Pāñcarātra Āgamas are a conti-nuation of the Vedic tradition. They also expand and expound the concepts about God and devotion.
Apart from सृष्टि (creation), sthiti (sustenance) and प्रलय (dissolution) of the world, God discharges two more functions: nigraha (controlling and punishing the evil-doers) and anugraha (showering his blessings on those who lead a good life and are devoted to him).
If the doctrine of भक्ति or devotion and प्रपत्ति or self-surrender find an important place in this system, no less is the attention paid to rituals, worship, images of deities and temples as also several mantras, the repetition of which will confer many a blessing on the votaries.
Thus the Pāñcarātra Āgamas have contributed considerably towards practical हिन्दुइस्म्. Even today, most of the Vaiṣṇava temples, especially in South India, follow their dictates, thus keeping those traditions alive.

Pañcabrahmamantras
(‘five mantras concerning five aspects of ब्रह्मन्’)
------------------------------------------
Though ब्रह्मा, विष्णु and महेश्वर (or शिव) are often described as the three aspects of the Supreme ब्रह्मन् (God, the Absolute), each one of them also is sometimes praised as ब्रह्मन् Himself.
In one such description, the five mantras on the five aspects of शिव given in the Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad (sections 17 to 21) are known as ‘Pañcabrahma-mantras’. The five aspects are: सद्योजात, वामदेव, अघोर, महादेव and ईशान.
Sometimes, these are shown as five faces of one and the same शिव.
These mantras are employed in the worship and meditation of महादेव with these five faces.

pañcasaṁskāras
(‘five rites of reformation’)
------------------------------------------
The Hindus can generally be divided into three broad groups: the śaivas (worshippers of शिव and allied deities like गणपति and सुब्रह्मण्य), the śāktas (worshippers of the मोथेर्-goddess) and the vaiṣṇavas (worshippers of विष्णु and his various aspects).
Among the ब्राह्मण followers of वैष्णविस्म्, there are two prominent groups: the śrīvaiṣṇavas and the vaiṣṇa-vas. The former are the followers of Rāmānuja (A.
-1137) whereas the latter are of Madhva (A.

-1317).
Every श्रीवैष्णव is expected to undergo five purificatory sacraments known as the पञ्चसṁस्कारस्. These help him to become fit enough to worship God.
They are: tāpa, पुण्ड्र, nāma, मन्त्र and याग.
Tāpa is also called ‘taptamudrā-dhāraṇa’. It is ब्रन्दिन्ग् one’s arms with the marks of शङ्ख (conch) and चक्र (discus), the two important symbols of Lord विष्णु. The permanent marks left on the body can constantly remind him that he now belongs to Lord विष्णु.
Puṇḍra is the religious mark—one U-line in white clay with a red line of vermillion or turmeric powder in between. This gives him a sense of belonging to the श्रीवैष्णव sect and also reminds him about the spiritual disciplines he has to follow, since this mark represents the three famous nāḍīs—iḍā, पिङ्गला and suṣumnā—described in the treatises on योग.
Nāma is the acceptance of a new name for himself such as Kṛṣṇadāsa or Viṣṇudāsa, that signifies the beginning of a new life as the servant of God.
Mantra is receiving through spiritual initiation from a qualified गुरु, a well-known name of God or formula like the अष्टाक्षरी, for जप (repetition) and upāsanā (meditation and worship).
After these four requirements are fulfilled, the sādhaka or the spiritual aspirant is expected to perform all his duties in a spirit of sacrifice and as a worship of God. He should strictly avoid all actions forbidden by the scriptures. This is called ‘yāga’.
A person becomes a true श्रीवैष्णव only after undergoing these pañca-सṁस्कारस्.
